claim: The germline genome of Tetrahymena thermophila is 157 Mb in length.
source: The final assembly is 157 Mb in length and composed of 1464 scaffolds, whereas the MAC genome assembly is 103 Mb and contains 1158 scaffolds.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the size of the MIC genome assembly based on sequencing and assembly data.

claim: The somatic (MAC) genome of Tetrahymena thermophila is 103 Mb in length.
source: The final assembly is 157 Mb in length and composed of 1464 scaffolds, whereas the MAC genome assembly is 103 Mb and contains 1158 scaffolds.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the size of the MAC genome assembly.

claim: Approximately one third (54 Mb) of the MIC genome is eliminated during MAC development.
source: We showed that approximately one third (54 Mb) of the MIC genome is eliminated in the form of around 12,000 IESs
evidence: The manuscript reports the amount of DNA eliminated based on comparison of MIC and MAC genome assemblies.

claim: There are approximately 12,000 Internal Eliminated Sequences (IESs) in the Tetrahymena thermophila MIC genome.
source: We showed that approximately one third (54 Mb) of the MIC genome is eliminated in the form of around 12,000 IESs
evidence: The manuscript reports the estimated total number of IESs based on genome-wide identification methods.

claim: The five MIC chromosomes are fragmented into about 200 MAC chromosomes.
source: In the widely studied model organism, Tetrahymena thermophila, the five MIC chromosomes are fragmented at sites of the 15 bp Chromosome breakage sequence (Cbs) (Yao et al., 1990) into about 200 MAC chromosomes (Eisen et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature for the number of MAC chromosomes generated from MIC chromosomes.

claim: The Chromosome breakage sequence (Cbs) is a 15 bp sequence that directs chromosome fragmentation in Tetrahymena thermophila.
source: In the widely studied model organism, Tetrahymena thermophila, the five MIC chromosomes are fragmented at sites of the 15 bp Chromosome breakage sequence (Cbs) (Yao et al., 1990) into about 200 MAC chromosomes (Eisen et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature establishing Cbs as the breakage signal.

claim: 225 Cbs sequences were identified in the MIC genome assembly.
source: We identified 225 Cbs's in the MIC genome assembly (Supplementary file 2A), including those associated with the ends of every MAC chromosome (Supplementary file 2B)
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of Cbs sequences identified through genome-wide analysis.

claim: The Cbs family is responsible for all developmentally programmed chromosome breakage in T. thermophila.
source: We identified 225 Cbs's in the MIC genome assembly (Supplementary file 2A), including those associated with the ends of every MAC chromosome (Supplementary file 2B); thus, the Cbs family is responsible for all developmentally programmed chromosome breakage in T. thermophila.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observation that Cbs sequences are found at all MAC chromosome ends.

claim: Nearly half (109 of 225) of the Cbs sequences have the consensus C-rich strand sequence: 5'-TAAACCAACCTCTTT-3'.
source: Nearly half the 225 Cbs's have the consensus C-rich strand sequence: 5'-TAAACCAACCTCTTT-3', and none has more than two substitutions to this sequence (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence analysis results showing the consensus sequence frequency.

claim: No Cbs has more than two substitutions from the consensus sequence.
source: Nearly half the 225 Cbs's have the consensus C-rich strand sequence: 5'-TAAACCAACCTCTTT-3', and none has more than two substitutions to this sequence (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the maximum number of substitutions observed in Cbs sequences.

claim: Ten of the 15 nucleotide positions in Cbs are completely conserved.
source: Confirming earlier studies (Hamilton et al., 2006b), 10 of the 15 nucleotide positions are completely conserved, while five show limited degeneracy
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence conservation analysis results and cites earlier studies.

claim: The Cbs consensus sequence can be summarized as 5'-WAAACCAACCYCNHW-3' (W = A or T; Y = C or T; H = A, C or T; N = any nucleotide).
source: Confirming earlier studies (Hamilton et al., 2006b), 10 of the 15 nucleotide positions are completely conserved, while five show limited degeneracy, summarized as follows: 5'-WAAACCAACCYCNHW-3' (W = A or T; Y = C or T; H = A, C or T; N = any nucleotide; Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the consensus sequence with degeneracy notation based on sequence analysis.

claim: The five putative centromeric regions range between 5.0 and 10.3 Mb in length.
source: The five putative centromeric regions range between 5.0 and 10.3 Mb and together comprise 37.8 Mb, or 24.7% of the assembled MIC genome.
evidence: The manuscript reports the size range of centromeric regions based on deletion mapping data.

claim: The five putative centromeric regions together comprise 37.8 Mb, or 24.7% of the assembled MIC genome.
source: The five putative centromeric regions range between 5.0 and 10.3 Mb and together comprise 37.8 Mb, or 24.7% of the assembled MIC genome.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total size and percentage of centromeric regions based on deletion mapping.

claim: Putative TEs and their remnants make up approximately 18.6 Mb (12.6%) of the total MIC genome assembly.
source: This annotation revealed that putative TEs and their remnants make up approximately 18.6 Mb (12.6%) of the total MIC genome assembly, and 10.9 Mb (41.7%) of the high-confidence IES set (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1, 2 and 3, Supplementary files 3B, 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports TE content based on repeat annotation analysis.

claim: Putative TEs make up 10.9 Mb (41.7%) of the high-confidence IES set.
source: This annotation revealed that putative TEs and their remnants make up approximately 18.6 Mb (12.6%) of the total MIC genome assembly, and 10.9 Mb (41.7%) of the high-confidence IES set (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1, 2 and 3, Supplementary files 3B, 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports TE content within IESs based on annotation analysis.

claim: About 95% of putative TE sequences are removed through IES excision during MAC development.
source: Although 95% of putative TE sequences are removed through IES excision during the development of the new MAC, about 1 Mb of putative TE sequences appear to be retained in the MAC (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of TE sequences eliminated based on comparison of MIC and MAC genomes.

claim: About 1 Mb of putative TE sequences appear to be retained in the MAC.
source: Although 95% of putative TE sequences are removed through IES excision during the development of the new MAC, about 1 Mb of putative TE sequences appear to be retained in the MAC (Figure 6A; Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the amount of TE sequences retained in the MAC based on genome analysis.

claim: The vast majority of classified putative TEs corresponds to class 2 (DNA) transposons, representing 48.7% of the repeated DNA in the MIC.
source: Among all classified putative TEs, the vast majority corresponds to class 2 (DNA) transposons, which represent 48.7% of the repeated DNA in the MIC (Figure 6B; Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the classification and abundance of DNA transposons based on TE annotation.

claim: No LTR retrotransposons were found in the Tetrahymena MIC genome.
source: Indeed, a small number (4.75% of the repeated DNA in the MIC) of non-LTR elements (mostly long interspersed nuclear elements, LINEs) was identified, but we found no evidence for the presence of any LTR retrotransposons.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of LTR retrotransposons based on TE annotation analysis.

claim: The high-confidence IES set contains 7551 IESs corresponding to 28.6 Mb of MIC DNA.
source: To allow analyses of elements with precisely defined endpoints, we built a 'high confidence' set of 7551 IESs (Supplementary file 3A). These IESs correspond to 28.6 Mb of MIC DNA
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and total size of high-confidence IESs.

claim: High-confidence IESs range in length from 136 bp to 43.4 kb.
source: These IESs correspond to 28.6 Mb of MIC DNA and range in length from 136 bp to 43.4 kb, with about 85% between 1 and 10 kb in length (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; mean = 3.78 kb; median = 2.78 kb).
evidence: The manuscript reports the size range of IESs based on genome-wide analysis.

claim: About 85% of high-confidence IESs are between 1 and 10 kb in length.
source: These IESs correspond to 28.6 Mb of MIC DNA and range in length from 136 bp to 43.4 kb, with about 85% between 1 and 10 kb in length (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; mean = 3.78 kb; median = 2.78 kb).
evidence: The manuscript reports the size distribution of IESs based on analysis.

claim: The mean length of high-confidence IESs is 3.78 kb.
source: These IESs correspond to 28.6 Mb of MIC DNA and range in length from 136 bp to 43.4 kb, with about 85% between 1 and 10 kb in length (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; mean = 3.78 kb; median = 2.78 kb).
evidence: The manuscript reports the mean IES length based on statistical analysis.

claim: The median length of high-confidence IESs is 2.78 kb.
source: These IESs correspond to 28.6 Mb of MIC DNA and range in length from 136 bp to 43.4 kb, with about 85% between 1 and 10 kb in length (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; mean = 3.78 kb; median = 2.78 kb).
evidence: The manuscript reports the median IES length based on statistical analysis.

claim: Virtually all high-confidence IESs are removed from predicted intergenic (82%) and intronic (16%) regions.
source: As expected, virtually all the high-confidence IESs are removed from predicted intergenic (6182, 82%) and intronic (1168, 16%) regions, where imprecise excision would not cripple gene function.
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of IESs by genomic location based on annotation analysis.

claim: Six solid cases of coding region IESs were identified.
source: We identified six solid cases of coding region IESs, described further below.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of coding region IESs identified through detailed analysis.

claim: The six coding region IESs are all flanked by TTAA terminal direct repeats.
source: First, all six are flanked by TTAA terminal direct repeats (TDRs), one copy of which is retained in the MAC; this sequence feature is shared by only 2% of all Tetrahymena IESs.
evidence: The manuscript reports the sequence features of coding region IESs based on analysis.

claim: The six coding region IESs have a distinctive terminal inverted repeat (TIR) with a consensus of 5'- CACTTT-3'.
source: Second, these six IESs have a distinctive terminal inverted repeat (TIR), internal to the TTAA direct repeat, with a consensus of 5'- CACTTT-3' (Figure 8B, Supplementary file 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the TIR consensus sequence based on sequence analysis.

claim: The six coding region IESs are all exceptionally short, including the three shortest IESs identified (136, 188 and 194 bp).
source: Third, the six coding region IESs are all exceptionally short; in fact, they include the three shortest IESs we identified (136, 188 and 194 bp, Supplementary file 3D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the sizes of coding region IESs based on sequence analysis.

claim: The six coding region IESs share the feature of exceptionally precise excision.
source: Finally, these six IESs share the feature of exceptionally precise excision (as determined in the study of excision variability described above), as would be expected in order to maintain correct protein-coding capacity.
evidence: The manuscript reports the excision precision based on variability analysis.

claim: 33 Non-Maintained Chromosomes (NMCs) were identified genome-wide.
source: Using our MIC chromosome super-assemblies, we identified a total of 33 NMCs (Supplementary file 2F), operationally defined as MIC DNA segments delimited by two consecutive Cbs's and absent from the MAC genome assembly.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of NMCs identified through genome-wide analysis.

claim: 47 predicted genes were identified distributed among 10 NMCs greater than 1 kb in length.
source: We identified 47 predicted genes, distributed among 10 NMCs (Supplementary file 2G).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of genes found in NMCs based on annotation.

claim: All 20 NMCs longer than 1 kb have acquired telomeres in exconjugants at 24 hr post-mixing.
source: We demonstrated that, in exconjugants at 24 hr post-mixing, all 20 NMCs longer than 1 kb have acquired telomeres (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results on telomere addition to NMCs.

claim: Roughly 80% (26/33) of NMCs have Cbs's from the same clade on both sides.
source: Recent Cbs duplication appears to be intimately connected to the evolutionary origin of most currently observed NMCs; roughly 80% (26/33) of NMCs have Cbs's from the same clade on both sides (Supplementary file 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of NMCs with clonal Cbs sequences based on sequence analysis.

claim: More than a third (13/33) of NMCs are short (1 kb or less) and contain no predicted genes.
source: More than a third (13/33) of NMCs are short (1 kb or less) and contain no predicted genes
evidence: The manuscript reports the size and gene content of a subset of NMCs.

claim: 49 Cbs-containing segments have at least one duplicate in the MIC genome.
source: Forty-nine Cbs-containing segments (23% of the 225) have at least one duplicate in the MIC genome.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of duplicated Cbs-containing segments based on sequence analysis.

claim: The 49 Cbs-containing segment duplicates cluster into 15 sequence similarity groups (clades).
source: The 49 Cbs-containing segment duplicates cluster into 15 sequence similarity groups (Supplementary file 2E; summarized in Table 3), which we call 'clades', to suggest that all members of each group were derived by successive duplications of an ancestral Cbs-containing segment.
evidence: The manuscript reports the clustering results based on sequence similarity analysis.

claim: MAC chromosome ends were highly conserved in all four Tetrahymena species studied.
source: Strikingly, MAC chromosome ends were highly conserved in all four species, indicating strong conservation of breakage sites.
evidence: The manuscript reports conservation results from comparative analysis of four species.

claim: With just one exception in T. borealis, the location of every chromosome breakage site in the four species has remained identical since their divergence.
source: Indeed, with just one exception in T. borealis, the location of every chromosome breakage site in the four species has remained identical since their divergence, down to the MIC genome interval between the same two consecutive homologous genes (Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the conservation of breakage site locations based on comparative analysis.

claim: The greatest number of IES junction sites (28%) displayed no terminal direct repeats (TDRs).
source: The greatest number of IES junction sites (28%) displayed no TDRs, and another 47% displayed TDRs of between 1 and 4 bp (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of TDRs at IES junctions based on sequence analysis.

claim: 47% of IES junction sites displayed TDRs of between 1 and 4 bp.
source: The greatest number of IES junction sites (28%) displayed no TDRs, and another 47% displayed TDRs of between 1 and 4 bp (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of short TDRs based on sequence analysis.

claim: TDRs at IES junctions are more AT-rich than immediately adjacent regions.
source: These TDRs are more AT-rich than immediately adjacent regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B), but include a wide diversity of sequences, with minimal bias (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the nucleotide composition of TDRs based on sequence analysis.

claim: Progeny IES excision endpoints were most often identical to those of the parent (26.6%).
source: Progeny endpoints were most often identical to those of the parent (26.6%), with most variations (83.3%) falling within 20 bp of the parental position (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of identical endpoints based on sequencing analysis of progeny.

claim: Most progeny IES excision endpoint variations (83.3%) fall within 20 bp of the parental position.
source: Progeny endpoints were most often identical to those of the parent (26.6%), with most variations (83.3%) falling within 20 bp of the parental position (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of endpoint variations based on sequencing analysis.

claim: The MIC genome assembly is composed of 1464 scaffolds.
source: The final assembly is 157 Mb in length and composed of 1464 scaffolds, whereas the MAC genome assembly is 103 Mb and contains 1158 scaffolds.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of scaffolds in the MIC assembly.

claim: The MAC genome assembly contains 1158 scaffolds.
source: The final assembly is 157 Mb in length and composed of 1464 scaffolds, whereas the MAC genome assembly is 103 Mb and contains 1158 scaffolds.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of scaffolds in the MAC assembly.

claim: The five MIC chromosome super-assemblies incorporate 152 Mb of the total 157 Mb MIC assembly.
source: The five chromosome super-assemblies incorporate 765 of the 1464 total MIC scaffolds, but because most of the unincorporated scaffolds are small (83% < 10 kb; Supplementary file 1C), the super-assemblies account for 152 Mb of the 157 Mb total MIC assembly length.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total length of the super-assemblies.

claim: The five MIC chromosome super-assemblies incorporate 765 of the 1464 total MIC scaffolds.
source: The five chromosome super-assemblies incorporate 765 of the 1464 total MIC scaffolds, but because most of the unincorporated scaffolds are small (83% < 10 kb; Supplementary file 1C), the super-assemblies account for 152 Mb of the 157 Mb total MIC assembly length.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of scaffolds incorporated into super-assemblies.

claim: 83% of unincorporated MIC scaffolds are less than 10 kb in length.
source: The five chromosome super-assemblies incorporate 765 of the 1464 total MIC scaffolds, but because most of the unincorporated scaffolds are small (83% < 10 kb; Supplementary file 1C), the super-assemblies account for 152 Mb of the 157 Mb total MIC assembly length.
evidence: The manuscript reports the size distribution of unincorporated scaffolds.

claim: Contamination of MIC sequencing libraries with MAC DNA was estimated to be less than 2%.
source: By microscopic counting of purified nuclei (taking into account the relative nuclear ploidy), we estimate that contamination with macronuclear genomic DNA was less than 2%.
evidence: The manuscript reports the estimated contamination level based on microscopic counting.

claim: The MIC genome was assembled with 169-fold sequence coverage.
source: The MIC genome was assembled with 169-fold sequence coverage using roughly an equal mix of fragment and mate-pair read data.
evidence: The manuscript reports the sequencing coverage used for assembly.

claim: Sequencing generated a total of approximately 125 Gb of data for the MIC genome.
source: Sequencing generated a total of approximately 125 Gb of data.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total amount of sequencing data generated.

claim: The MAC genome has a ploidy of about 45N for all but one chromosome in Tetrahymena.
source: It has been suggested that the evolutionary advantage of chromosome fragmentation may relate to the high ploidy of MACs (~45N for all but one chromosome in Tetrahymena, ~800 N in Paramecium, ~2000 N in Oxytricha) and their amitotic division mechanism
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about MAC ploidy in Tetrahymena.

claim: Paramecium MAC has a ploidy of about 800N.
source: It has been suggested that the evolutionary advantage of chromosome fragmentation may relate to the high ploidy of MACs (~45N for all but one chromosome in Tetrahymena, ~800 N in Paramecium, ~2000 N in Oxytricha) and their amitotic division mechanism
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about MAC ploidy in Paramecium.

claim: Oxytricha MAC has a ploidy of about 2000N.
source: It has been suggested that the evolutionary advantage of chromosome fragmentation may relate to the high ploidy of MACs (~45N for all but one chromosome in Tetrahymena, ~800 N in Paramecium, ~2000 N in Oxytricha) and their amitotic division mechanism
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about MAC ploidy in Oxytricha.

claim: Paramecium tetraurelia has about 45,000 short, unique copy IESs.
source: In Paramecium tetraurelia, a fellow oligohymenophorean ciliate distantly related to Tetrahymena (Baroin-Tourancheau et al., 1992), partial assembly of the MIC genome has revealed the presence of about 45,000 short, unique copy IESs, many lying within the MIC progenitors of MAC genes (Arnaiz et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Paramecium IES numbers.

claim: Oxytricha trifallax has roughly 16,000 MAC chromosomes.
source: Roughly 16,000 MAC chromosomes (most carrying only a single gene) (Swart et al., 2013) are derived from a MIC genome ten times the size of the MAC genome
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Oxytricha chromosome numbers.

claim: The Oxytricha MIC genome is ten times the size of the MAC genome.
source: Roughly 16,000 MAC chromosomes (most carrying only a single gene) (Swart et al., 2013) are derived from a MIC genome ten times the size of the MAC genome
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Oxytricha genome sizes.

claim: IES elimination in Tetrahymena requires the action of proteins domesticated from piggyBac transposases.
source: In both Tetrahymena and Paramecium, IES elimination requires the action of proteins domesticated from piggyBac transposases (Baudry et al., 2009; Cheng et al., 2010; Shieh and Chalker, 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on the role of domesticated transposases in IES elimination.

claim: IES elimination in Paramecium requires the action of proteins domesticated from piggyBac transposases.
source: In both Tetrahymena and Paramecium, IES elimination requires the action of proteins domesticated from piggyBac transposases (Baudry et al., 2009; Cheng et al., 2010; Shieh and Chalker, 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on the role of domesticated transposases in IES elimination.

claim: Ciliates carry two distinct nuclei that display a remarkable form of germline/soma differentiation.
source: Although unicellular, ciliates carry two distinct nuclei that display a remarkable form of germline/soma differentiation (Figure 1A; Orias et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on ciliate nuclear differentiation.

claim: The micronucleus (MIC) is the smaller, diploid, transcriptionally silent germline nucleus.
source: the smaller, diploid, transcriptionally silent germline nucleus (micronucleus or MIC) contains the genetic material transmitted across sexual generations
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of the MIC based on established knowledge.

claim: The macronucleus (MAC) is the larger, polyploid, actively expressed somatic nucleus.
source: whereas the larger, polyploid, actively expressed somatic nucleus (macronucleus or MAC) supports all the vegetative functions of the cell.
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of the MAC based on established knowledge.

claim: The MAC is derived from a mitotic sibling of the MIC during sexual reproduction.
source: Despite differing in several fundamental features of eukaryotic nuclei, the MAC is derived from a mitotic sibling of the MIC during sexual reproduction in a process that involves extensive, genome-wide programmed DNA rearrangements.
evidence: The manuscript describes the developmental origin of the MAC based on established knowledge.

claim: Cbs is a necessary and sufficient cis-acting DNA element for chromosome breakage in T. thermophila.
source: Tetrahymena carries out chromosome breakage and telomere addition with high specificity and reliability. In T. thermophila and related species (Coyne and Yao, 1996), these processes are driven by the necessary and sufficient cis-acting DNA element, Cbs (Chromosome breakage sequence), a highly conserved 15-mer (Fan and Yao, 2000; Hamilton et al., 2006b; Yao et al., 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature establishing Cbs as necessary and sufficient for breakage.

claim: De novo telomere addition by telomerase occurs within a region ~5–25 bp on each side of a Cbs.
source: De novo telomere addition by telomerase occurs within a region ~5–25 bp on each side of a Cbs (Fan and Yao, 1996)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on the location of telomere addition relative to Cbs.

claim: The Cbs itself and its immediate flanking sequences are found only in the MIC.
source: De novo telomere addition by telomerase occurs within a region ~5–25 bp on each side of a Cbs (Fan and Yao, 1996); the Cbs itself and its immediate flanking sequences are found only in the MIC.
evidence: The manuscript states that Cbs sequences are MIC-specific based on genome comparisons.

claim: Seven complex MAC chromosomes are generated by site-specific joining of non-contiguous segments of germline DNA.
source: However, we identified seven complex MAC chromosomes that are generated not simply by conventional fragmentation, but also by the site-specific joining of non-contiguous segments of germline DNA.
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of complex chromosomes based on genome analysis.

claim: The non-contiguity of complex MAC chromosomes has been experimentally confirmed for three cases.
source: The non-contiguity has been experimentally confirmed for three cases, eliminating the possibility that they are genome assembly artifacts.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental confirmation of non-contiguous joining.

claim: Every functional Cbs contains a permuted copy (C2A2C2) of the T. thermophila telomeric repeat C4A2.
source: As previously noted for the consensus sequence (Yao et al., 1987), every functional Cbs contains a permuted copy (C2A2C2) of the T. thermophila telomeric repeat C4A2.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature and confirms the presence of telomeric repeat sequences in Cbs.

claim: The Cbs consensus shares with Tetrahymena telomeric repeats a striking C vs. G strand asymmetry.
source: More generally, the Cbs consensus shares with Tetrahymena telomeric repeats a striking C vs. G strand asymmetry
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence analysis showing strand asymmetry.

claim: Of the 117 non-consensus functional Cbs sequences, only one contains a substitution on the C-rich strand to a G (at position 13) whereas 27 contain a substitution to C.
source: of the 117 non-consensus functional Cbs sequences, only one contains a substitution on the C-rich strand to a G (at position 13) whereas 27 contain a substitution to C (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of substitutions based on sequence analysis.

claim: The likelihood of the observed C vs. G substitution ratio being due to chance alone is low (probability of chi square << 0.01).
source: The likelihood of this ratio being due to chance alone is low (probability of chi square << 0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of substitution patterns.

claim: Pot2p is the first factor shown to associate specifically with Cbs regions in vivo, at the time of chromosome breakage.
source: Pot2p is the first factor shown to associate specifically with Cbs regions in vivo, at the time of chromosome breakage (Cranert et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Pot2p association with Cbs.

claim: Pot2p is a paralog of Pot1p, which is required for telomere maintenance.
source: Pot2p is a paralog of Pot1p, which is required for telomere maintenance.
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about Pot2p and Pot1p relationship.

claim: Repetitive sequences and putative TEs are more prevalent in the putative centromeric regions than in the chromosome arms.
source: We plotted the densities along each MIC chromosome of both simple sequence repeats (Figure 2, purple lines) and putative TEs and their remnants (blue lines; see below for a description of TE characterization) and found that both types of repetitive sequence are more prevalent in the putative centromeric regions than in the chromosome arms.
evidence: The manuscript reports density analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The central regions of MIC chromosomes span approximately 7 to 12 Mb or about one quarter to one third of the chromosome lengths.
source: The central regions, spanning approximately 7 to 12 Mb or about one quarter to one third of the chromosome lengths, share essentially the same range as the repeat-rich putative centromeric regions identified above.
evidence: The manuscript reports the size range of central regions based on chromosome super-assemblies.

claim: Early-scnRNAs are produced primarily from shorter MIC scaffolds.
source: Early-scnRNAs are produced primarily from shorter MIC scaffolds, whereas Late-scnRNAs originate from both large and small MIC scaffolds
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on scnRNA origins.

claim: Late-scnRNAs originate from both large and small MIC scaffolds.
source: Early-scnRNAs are produced primarily from shorter MIC scaffolds, whereas Late-scnRNAs originate from both large and small MIC scaffolds
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on scnRNA origins.

claim: Early-scnRNA primarily map to the middle and end regions of MIC chromosomes.
source: We found that, whereas Late-scnRNAs originate from locations throughout the MIC chromosomes (Figure 7B), Early-scnRNA primarily map to the middle and end regions (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript reports mapping results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Late-scnRNAs originate from locations throughout the MIC chromosomes.
source: We found that, whereas Late-scnRNAs originate from locations throughout the MIC chromosomes (Figure 7B), Early-scnRNA primarily map to the middle and end regions (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript reports mapping results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The increased number of IESs in the middle and end regions does not fully explain the enrichment of Early-scnRNAs in these regions.
source: The increased number of IESs in these regions (Figure 2) does not fully explain this phenomenon, because many IESs are located within chromosomal arm regions, but most do not give rise to Early-scnRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from comparing IES and scnRNA distributions.

claim: Some yet unknown mechanism restricts production of Early-scnRNAs to the central and terminal chromosome regions.
source: We conclude some yet unknown mechanism restricts production of Early-scnRNAs to the central and terminal chromosome regions.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the observed distribution patterns.

claim: Tetrahymena IES excision occurs by a transposase-related mechanism initiated by a staggered, double-strand break.
source: Biochemical studies suggest that Tetrahymena IES excision occurs by a transposase-related mechanism initiated by a staggered, double-strand break (Saveliev and Cox, 1996, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous biochemical studies on IES excision mechanism.

claim: Previous small-scale studies have shown that Tetrahymena IES breakpoints do not share a strong consensus sequence and display frequent heterogeneity.
source: Previous small-scale studies have shown that breakpoints do not share a strong consensus sequence and display frequent heterogeneity (Austerberry et al., 1989; Li and Pearlman, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on IES breakpoint characteristics.

claim: The domesticated piggyBac transposase Tpb2p is required in vivo for IES excision.
source: The domesticated piggyBac transposase Tpb2p, required in vivo for IES excision, can introduce breaks in vitro of the expected geometry, and with a relaxed sequence preference (Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Tpb2p function.

claim: Tpb2p can introduce breaks in vitro of the expected geometry, and with a relaxed sequence preference.
source: The domesticated piggyBac transposase Tpb2p, required in vivo for IES excision, can introduce breaks in vitro of the expected geometry, and with a relaxed sequence preference (Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Tpb2p biochemical properties.

claim: The great majority of IES sites exhibited variability in excision endpoints, with up to 14 different junctions per site.
source: Nevertheless, even using conservative validation criteria, the great majority of IES sites exhibited variability, with up to 14 different junctions per site (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports variability analysis results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Nearly all IESs exhibited some endpoint variability upon closer visual inspection of alignment data.
source: Even for IESs that at first appeared to have no, or exceptionally low, variability, closer visual inspection of alignment data revealed that nearly all exhibited some endpoint variability.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from detailed inspection of sequencing data.

claim: The scnRNA-mediated genome rearrangement mechanism involves whole genome comparison of the parental and newly developing MACs.
source: The scnRNA-mediated genome rearrangement mechanism involves whole genome comparison of the parental and newly developing MACs, with the state of the pre-rearranged parental genome influencing events in the progeny in a locus-specific manner (Mochizuki and Gorovsky, 2004; Yao and Chao, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on the scnRNA-mediated mechanism.

claim: The progeny endpoint distribution shows a small spike at a distance of 4 bp from the parental endpoint.
source: The progeny endpoint distribution shows a small spike at a distance of 4 bp from the parental endpoint.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of endpoint distribution patterns.

claim: The spike at 4 bp distance would be consistent with the use of the same breakpoint, followed by differential repair of the four base overhang generated by Tpb2p.
source: This would be consistent with the use of the same breakpoint, followed by differential repair of the four base overhang generated by Tpb2p, using either the 'right' or 'left' overhang as template.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation based on the observed pattern and known Tpb2p activity.

claim: In Paramecium, the TA dinucleotide central to the four nucleotide overhang is invariant.
source: However, in contrast to the junctional diversity observed in Tetrahymena, the TA dinucleotide central to the four nucleotide overhang is invariant (Arnaiz et al., 2012; Gratias and Bétermier, 2003)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Paramecium IES junction sequences.

claim: Excision endpoint variability in Paramecium is extremely low.
source: However, in contrast to the junctional diversity observed in Tetrahymena, the TA dinucleotide central to the four nucleotide overhang is invariant (Arnaiz et al., 2012; Gratias and Bétermier, 2003) and excision endpoint variability is extremely low.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Paramecium excision precision.

claim: The invariant TA dinucleotide has allowed Paramecium IESs to frequently occupy protein-coding regions.
source: These features have allowed Paramecium IESs to frequently occupy protein-coding regions, whereas the imprecision of Tpb2p and the near total absence of IESs in Tetrahymena protein-coding regions have most likely co-evolved to result in a strikingly different MIC genome landscape.
evidence: The manuscript infers this evolutionary relationship from comparing Paramecium and Tetrahymena.

claim: The imprecision of Tpb2p and the near total absence of IESs in Tetrahymena protein-coding regions have most likely co-evolved.
source: These features have allowed Paramecium IESs to frequently occupy protein-coding regions, whereas the imprecision of Tpb2p and the near total absence of IESs in Tetrahymena protein-coding regions have most likely co-evolved to result in a strikingly different MIC genome landscape.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this evolutionary hypothesis based on comparative analysis.

claim: The TIR of the six coding region IESs resembles that of PiggyBac TEs of several species.
source: This TIR resembles that of PiggyBac TEs of several species (as found in RepBase: http://www.girinst.org/repbase/index.html and (Xu et al., 2006)
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence similarity to known piggyBac TEs.

claim: The TIR of the six coding region IESs also resembles the two full-length piggyBac consensus sequences annotated in the Tetrahymena MIC genome.
source: and also the two full-length piggyBac consensus sequences annotated in the Tetrahymena MIC genome (Figure 6—source datas 1; 5'-CCCT(A/T)T-3' for Contig[0117] and 5'-CCC(A/T)(C/T)T-3' for R = 3481).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence similarity to piggyBac elements in the MIC genome.

claim: Apart from their size and terminal sequences, no other conserved sequence features were detected within or flanking the six coding region IESs.
source: Apart from their size and terminal sequences, no other conserved sequence features were detected, either within or flanking the IESs.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of sequence analysis.

claim: Tpb2p exhibits very little sequence specificity and wide variability.
source: It has been reported that Tpb2p exhibits very little sequence specificity and wide variability (Cheng et al., 2010; Vogt and Mochizuki, 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Tpb2p specificity.

claim: The expression of all five genes containing coding region IESs is conjugation-specific.
source: The expression of all five is conjugation-specific (Miao et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2012), peaking at approximately the same time point (8–10 hr post-mixing; http://tfgd.ihb.ac.cn/), near the time of IES excision.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on gene expression patterns.

claim: The expression of all five genes containing coding region IESs peaks at approximately 8–10 hr post-mixing, near the time of IES excision.
source: The expression of all five is conjugation-specific (Miao et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2012), peaking at approximately the same time point (8–10 hr post-mixing; http://tfgd.ihb.ac.cn/), near the time of IES excision.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature and databases on expression timing.

claim: The predicted protein sequences of genes containing coding region IESs contain functional domains of potential relevance to the regulation of gene function and/or MAC development.
source: In addition, the predicted protein sequences contain functional domains of potential relevance to the regulation of gene function and/or MAC development, including zinc finger, bromodomain, and DEAD-DEAH helicase (Lia2p).
evidence: The manuscript reports domain annotation results.

claim: The emergence of an efficient yet imprecise excision mechanism in Tetrahymena has driven selection against almost all coding region IESs that existed in a common ancestor of Tetrahymena and Paramecium.
source: Perhaps, the emergence of an efficient yet imprecise excision mechanism in Tetrahymena, based primarily on the epigenetic scnRNA mechanism to identify IESs and determine their boundaries, has driven selection against almost all coding region IESs that existed in a common ancestor of Tetrahymena and Paramecium, with the few remaining Tetrahymena cases persisting for gene regulatory purposes.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this evolutionary hypothesis based on comparative analysis.

claim: The few remaining Tetrahymena coding region IESs may persist for gene regulatory purposes.
source: Perhaps, the emergence of an efficient yet imprecise excision mechanism in Tetrahymena, based primarily on the epigenetic scnRNA mechanism to identify IESs and determine their boundaries, has driven selection against almost all coding region IESs that existed in a common ancestor of Tetrahymena and Paramecium, with the few remaining Tetrahymena cases persisting for gene regulatory purposes.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis about the function of coding region IESs.

claim: Comparisons between Tetrahymena, Paramecium, and Oxytricha reveal the extraordinary diversity and adaptability of ciliate germline/soma nuclear differentiation.
source: Consistent with the deep evolutionary branching of the phylum (Baroin-Tourancheau et al., 1992), comparisons between Tetrahymena, Paramecium, and Oxytricha reveals the extraordinary diversity and adaptability of ciliate germline/soma nuclear differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from comparative analysis and cites literature on phylogeny.

claim: The total DNA content within all identified IESs is around 46 Mb, accounting for 85% of the difference (54 Mb) between the MIC and MAC genome assemblies.
source: The total DNA content within all identified IESs is around 46 Mb, accounting for 85% of the difference (54 Mb) between the MIC and MAC genome assemblies.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total IES content based on genome-wide identification.

claim: The identification of IESs suggests that most MIC-limited regions are in the form of IESs.
source: This suggests that we have identified the majority of Tetrahymena IESs and that most MIC-limited regions are in the form of IESs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the proportion of MIC-MAC difference accounted for by IESs.

claim: The MIC genome is highly AT-rich (77.9%).
source: The T. thermophila germline genome is highly AT-rich (MAC assembly 77.7% and MIC assembly 77.9%)
evidence: The manuscript reports the nucleotide composition of the MIC genome.

claim: The MAC genome is highly AT-rich (77.7%).
source: The T. thermophila germline genome is highly AT-rich (MAC assembly 77.7% and MIC assembly 77.9%)
evidence: The manuscript reports the nucleotide composition of the MAC genome.

claim: MIC telomeres were not detected in the MIC genome scaffolds, suggesting that their repetitive nature prevented assembly.
source: MIC telomeres, which have a distinctive terminal repeat sequence as well as sub-telomeric repeats (Kirk and Blackburn, 1995), were not detected in the MIC genome scaffolds, suggesting that their repetitive nature prevented assembly.
evidence: The manuscript infers this explanation for the absence of telomeres in the assembly.

claim: Approximately 6.4% (constituting 10.0 Mb) of the MIC genome assembly consists of Ns (assembly gaps).
source: Because of the numerous gaps in the MIC genome assembly, approximately 6.4% (constituting 10.0 Mb) consists of Ns.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of assembly gaps.

claim: Unassembled parts of the MIC genome are likely to contain many more repeats than assembled regions.
source: Because repeat-rich sequences are difficult to assemble, the unassembled parts of the genome are likely to contain many more repeats.
evidence: The manuscript infers this based on known assembly challenges with repetitive sequences.

claim: There is a significant retention of repetitive sequences in the MAC.
source: Thus, as first described by Eisen et al. (2006), there is a significant retention of repetitive sequences in the MAC
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature and confirms retention of repeats in the MAC.

claim: It is not possible to determine what portion of MAC repetitive sequences are eliminated from the MIC genome.
source: but it is not possible to say what portion of these sequences are eliminated from the MIC genome.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation in determining the origin of MAC repeats.

claim: There is evidence of very recent amplifications for the most abundant DNA cut-and-paste transposon superfamilies.
source: Despite TEs being restricted to the transcriptionally silent MIC (Chalker et al., 2013; Coyne et al., 2012; Schoeberl and Mochizuki, 2011), we found evidence of very recent amplifications for the most abundant DNA cut-and-paste transposon superfamilies, based on the nearly identical sequences of some copies, as well as the presence of intact open-reading frames and terminal inverted repeats (see Materials and methods; Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports evidence of recent TE activity based on sequence analysis.

claim: The evidence suggests recent transpositional activity of multiple DNA transposon families within the MIC genome.
source: This suggests the recent transpositional activity of multiple DNA transposon families within the MIC genome.
evidence: The manuscript infers recent activity from sequence similarity and structural features.

claim: Over 60% of the unincorporated MIC scaffolds have no significant matches to the MAC assembly.
source: Over 60% of the unincorporated scaffolds have no significant matches to the MAC assembly.
evidence: The manuscript reports alignment results for unincorporated scaffolds.

claim: It appears all or nearly all the unincorporated MIC scaffolds are entirely MIC-specific.
source: Thus, it appears all or nearly all the unincorporated scaffolds are entirely MIC-specific.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from alignment analysis.

claim: Centromeric histone H3 disappears from differentiating MACs during formation of a new MAC in Tetrahymena.
source: During formation of a new MAC in Tetrahymena, the centromeric histone H3 disappears from differentiating MACs, suggesting the programmed elimination of Cen-specific sequences (Cervantes et al., 2006; Cui and Gorovsky, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on centromeric histone H3 dynamics.

claim: IES removal is sufficient to account for centromere loss in Tetrahymena.
source: The close, linear packing of MAC chromosome precursors along the entire length of MIC chromosomes and the presence of retained, macronuclear-destined sequences (MDSs) interspersed throughout the Tetrahymena centromere regions suggests that IES removal is sufficient to account for this centromere loss.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the distribution of MDSs in centromeric regions.

claim: Centromeric histone H3 disappears during MAC differentiation in Paramecium.
source: Centromeric histone H3 also disappears during MAC differentiation in Paramecium, and this disappearance is dependent on factors required for IES excision (Lhuillier-Akakpo et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature on Paramecium centromeric histone H3.

claim: The centromeres of both Tetrahymena and Paramecium are eliminated as IESs despite their apparent dissimilarities.
source: suggesting that the centromeres of both organisms, despite their apparent dissimilarities, are eliminated as IESs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from comparing centromere elimination in both organisms.

claim: MAC chromosomes derived from MIC centromeric regions tend to be unusually large.
source: We also note, as described in Supplementary file 1E, that MAC chromosomes derived from MIC centromeric regions tend to be unusually large.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation based on analysis of MAC chromosome sizes.

claim: The midpoints of the MIC chromosomes lie near the centromeric region midpoints.
source: Cytologically, all five Tetrahymena MIC chromosomes appear metacentric and, as expected, the midpoints of the chromosomal super-assembly lie near the centromeric region midpoints (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation based on cytological data and super-assembly analysis.

claim: The centromere regions of the MIC assembly are highly fragmented.
source: The centromere regions of the MIC assembly are highly fragmented (Table 1, column 5; Figure 2)
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation based on assembly analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Missing sequence in centromeric regions would increase their estimated size.
source: These estimates are subject to change in either direction for the following reasons. The centromere regions of the MIC assembly are highly fragmented (Table 1, column 5; Figure 2); missing sequence would increase their size.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation in size estimation.

claim: The complete region between flanking Cbs's may not be required for centromere function.
source: On the other hand, the precise endpoints of the deletions are unknown, and the complete region between flanking Cbs's may not be required for centromere function.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this uncertainty in defining centromere boundaries.
